parts.title: Passage 1 · Children in Crisis
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions and word limits shown on the book pages. Choose the requested letters or write your answers.

questions.explanation: Bystanders are onlookers who are present when an event happens without taking part.
questions.evidence: Bystanders are caught in the crossfire

questions.explanation: To become desensitised is to become less sensitive or less affected by something.
questions.evidence: so desensitised to shooting that they laugh about it

questions.explanation: Being charged with an offence means being formally accused of it. It does not itself mean being punished.
questions.evidence: charged with assault and attempted murder

questions.explanation: 'Sufficient' means enough for the stated purpose.
questions.evidence: sufficient education, motivations, and undamaged brains

questions.explanation: The passage names sneakers, leather jackets and insults as reasons for shootings.
questions.evidence: the reasons may be only sneakers, leather jackets, or insults

questions.explanation: It says robbing other people is regarded as a symbol of honour in many cities.
questions.evidence: robbing the others is considered a symbol of honour

questions.explanation: The passage describes the victims as strangers to their attackers, contradicting the idea that they usually knew them.
questions.evidence: The victims all appeared to be strangers to their torturers.

questions.explanation: The text says almost everyone agrees that many young criminals are becoming more violent, rather than describing widespread disagreement.
questions.evidence: Almost everyone agrees

questions.explanation: The organisation's report gives a daily figure for murders of children under five.
questions.evidence: two children under the age of five are murdered in America each day

questions.explanation: The text says some adults are unaware or do not want to be aware, but does not explicitly say fear is why they avoid knowing.
questions.evidence: Many adults are not, or do not want to be, aware

questions.explanation: Conservative magazines are described as normally giving more space to business than to social problems.
questions.evidence: devote their pages more to business than social problems

questions.explanation: Forbes is introduced as an example of the conservative magazines discussed in the preceding sentence.
questions.evidence: even conservative magazines ... For example, in one issue of Forbes magazine

questions.explanation: The summary refers to senseless juvenile crimes that seem to lack a reason or motive.
questions.evidence: senseless crimes done by juveniles that appear to lack a motive

questions.explanation: The example concerns homeless people sleeping in subway stations. These three words fit the summary's grammar.
questions.evidence: homeless men sleeping in subway stations

questions.explanation: The passage gives twenty as the number of attempts in 1992.
questions.evidence: as many as twenty times in 1992

questions.explanation: The phrase 'set fire to' supplies the two missing words before 'to them'.
questions.evidence: young people tried to set fire to homeless men

questions.explanation: The account is given by one of the people who set the fire.
questions.evidence: One fire setter explained

questions.explanation: The boy says the beer was spilled accidentally.
questions.evidence: accidentally spilled some of their beer on him

questions.explanation: It was the homeless man's blanket that caught fire.
questions.evidence: when his blanket caught fire

questions.explanation: The summary needs 'the fun' before 'of it'; the passage suggests amusement as a possible motive.
questions.evidence: the fun of it was suggested as a motive

parts.title: Passage 2 · Real-Time Electronic Discussion for Teaching Writing
parts.instructions: Follow the original instructions and word limits shown on the book pages. Choose the requested letters or write your answers.

questions.explanation: To compose a text means write it.
questions.evidence: compose compositions together

questions.explanation: 'Virtually all' means almost all.
questions.evidence: virtually all class discussion

questions.explanation: Transcripts are written or printed records of spoken discussions.
questions.evidence: transcripts of large group discussions

questions.explanation: To participate in a discussion means join in it.
questions.evidence: 100% of the students participated

questions.explanation: Being confident means feeling trust in one's ability.
questions.evidence: confident about their writing

questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes the writing as taking place in a powerful communicative context.
questions.evidence: such a powerful communicative context

questions.explanation: The stated purpose is sharing ideas with classmates.
questions.evidence: for the purpose of sharing ideas with their classmates

questions.explanation: Cook contributes as a guide, rather than an expert who supplies every answer.
questions.evidence: as a guide rather than as an all-knowing expert

questions.explanation: All students participated in the electronic discussion. The source asks for one word here but reports this result numerically, so the corresponding number is accepted.
questions.evidence: 100% of the students participated in the electronic discussion

questions.explanation: The electronic-discussion chart gives the students 65% of the turns. This also follows from the teacher's 35%: 100 minus 35 equals 65. The printed prompt already supplies 'percent'.
questions.evidence: the teacher took only 35% of the turns

questions.explanation: The study reports significantly greater gains in the computer-networked class's writing.
questions.evidence: showed significantly greater gains in writing

questions.explanation: The first paragraph explicitly presents electronic discussion as a way to overcome fear of writing.
questions.evidence: To help overcome this fear

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts sharing ideas with writing only for correction. It does not say students hate teacher correction.
questions.evidence: not for the purpose of being corrected ... sharing ideas

questions.explanation: Cook had taught online for three years and feared returning to non-networked instruction.
questions.evidence: She has taught this way for 3 years ... feared even the thought of going back

questions.explanation: The syllabus was the same, but only one class used networked discussion; the other used a traditional classroom.
questions.evidence: The other class was conducted in a traditional classroom

questions.explanation: Only half the traditional class spoke even once, meaning the other half remained silent in the discussion.
questions.evidence: only 50% of the students spoke up even once

questions.explanation: The text discusses benefits for native speakers and second-language students but does not compare their overall levels of confidence.
questions.evidence: Studies of native speaker composition classes have also shown similar advantages

questions.explanation: The final paragraph reports similar advantages in native-speaker classes, contradicting the claim that the method does not work there.
questions.evidence: have also shown similar advantages
